findings.explanation: The dynamic "containers" block has no startup_probe or liveness_probe, and the module exposes no variable for either - every consumer is stuck with Cloud Run's default startup behavior (a TCP check on the container port) regardless of what the workload actually needs. A TCP-open check passes the moment the process binds the port, which for anything with a real startup sequence (DB migrations, cache warmup, dependency checks) can route live traffic to an instance before it's actually ready to serve, and a missing liveness_probe means a hung-but-still-listening process is never automatically restarted.
findings.remediation: Add optional startup_probe/liveness_probe variables (e.g. var.startup_probe, var.liveness_probe as nullable objects mirroring the provider's http_get/tcp_socket/period_seconds/failure_threshold shape) and wire them into the containers dynamic block with dynamic sub-blocks guarded on non-null, the same pattern already used for vpc_access/empty_dir elsewhere in this file.
findings.title: No startup_probe/liveness_probe support - every deployment relies on Cloud Run's default TCP probe

findings.explanation: There's no scaling block anywhere in the template, and no variable exposes one - every service built with this module inherits Cloud Run's project-level default max instance count with no per-service ceiling. A traffic spike, a retry storm from a misbehaving caller, or a bug that causes self-referential requests (plausible here specifically, since examplemulti's frontend calls the backend service) scales container instances - and the bill - with nothing in the module stopping it.
findings.remediation: Add an optional var.max_instance_count (and ideally var.min_instance_count for the paired reliability concern in HOLDEN_BP_004) and a scaling { max_instance_count = ... } block inside template, defaulting to null/unset to preserve current behavior for existing callers.
findings.title: No way to cap max_instance_count - autoscaling is unbounded for every deployment

findings.explanation: Same gap as HOLDEN_BP_002 but on the min side: no scaling block and no variable means every service scales to zero when idle, so the first request after any idle period pays a full cold start (container scheduling + app init). For a latency-sensitive service (or one behind a synchronous caller, like examplemulti's frontend-to-backend call) this is a real UX/latency cost, not just a theoretical one - and there's currently no way for a caller of this module to opt out of it.
findings.remediation: Add an optional var.min_instance_count (default null, preserving scale-to-zero as the default) alongside HOLDEN_BP_002's max_instance_count, in the same scaling block.
findings.title: No way to configure min_instance_count - every deployment cold-starts from zero

findings.explanation: Both examples hardcode project = "pike-477416" directly on every resource/data source/module call (3 occurrences in examplea, 7 in examplemulti) instead of a single variable + tfvars. Anyone who clones these examples to try the module against their own project has to find-and-replace a literal string across multiple files rather than setting one value - the examples aren't reusable as a starting point without that manual edit, which undercuts their purpose as a demonstration a reader can actually run.
findings.fix:
In each example directory, add a variables.tf:

variable "project" {
  type        = string
  default     = "pike-477416"
  description = "GCP project ID to deploy the example into"
}

Then replace every literal "pike-477416" in that example's .tf files with var.project.
findings.remediation: Introduce a variable "project" (or reuse a project.auto.tfvars) in each example and replace every literal "pike-477416" with var.project.
findings.resource: example/examplea, example/examplemulti (10 occurrences of "pike-477416" across both)
findings.title: Examples hardcode the GCP project ID inline across 10 locations instead of a variable
